These reserves are netted against sales at the time of the related sale, impacting the company's profit and loss (P&L) by reducing reported net sales and, correspondingly, net income. If the actual coupon redemption rate deviates from the estimated rate used to set reserves, this can impact the P&L in future periods. For example, if the actual redemption rate is 0.1% higher than estimated, the required reserve would increase by approximately $0.7 million, reducing future net sales and profits. Conversely, if the redemption rate is lower, previously accrued reserves may be reversed, increasing net sales and profits. On cash flow, coupon reserve adjustments do not immediately affect cash, as cash outflows occur when coupons are actually redeemed and paid. However, changes in the reserve only impact cash flow if they result in higher or lower cash payments for coupon redemptions compared to accruals. Thus, variances between estimated and actual redemptions primarily affect the P&L, while the cash flow impact is realized as redemptions are paid out over time. In summary: - Coupon reserves reduce net sales and profit when accrued. - Redemption variances can lead to future P&L adjustments (either up or down). - Cash flow is affected only when actual coupon redemptions are paid, not when reserves are accrued or adjusted (Chunks 5, 6, 14).

Conversely, an overestimation (if redemption rates fall) can lead to lower expenses, potentially boosting profitability when adjustments or releases of excess reserves occur.
